cards.explanation: The answer is palace. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, has two projects on his mind: a house for the Name of the LORD and a royal palace for himself. The verse says he "purposed" to build both. I'd say that's a pretty big weekend of building.

The answer is cedars. Solomon, David's son, reminds Hiram, king of Tyre, of the favor he did for David before. Hiram sent David cedars so David could build himself a house to live in. Now Solomon is asking for the same kind of help, and when a plan worked once, it makes sense to go back to the same lumberyard.

The answer is every morning and evening. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, tells Hiram, king of Tyre, that the burnt offerings will be made every morning and evening. They'll also be made on the Sabbaths, New Moons and appointed feasts of the LORD. That's a steady rhythm, twice a day.

The answer is True. Solomon finishes his list of what the house is for with these words to Hiram, king of Tyre: "This is ordained for Israel forever." The incense, the showbread and the offerings are not a one-time event. They're meant to keep going, and Solomon wants Hiram to know what he's helping build.

The answer is because God is greater than all gods. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, doesn't brag about the building or his own power. He tells Hiram the house will be great, "…for our God is greater than all gods." The greatness comes from who the house is for, and that's the right place to put it.

The answer is that even the highest heavens cannot contain Him. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, asks, "But who is able to build a house for Him, since the heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain Him?" If the highest heavens can't hold God, no building can either. He knows it's a big job and an even bigger God, and he's humble about it.

The answer is True. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, asks Hiram, king of Tyre, to send "…a craftsman skilled in engraving…" He wants someone who can work with gold, silver, bronze, iron, and purple, crimson and blue yarn. That's a long list for one person, so Solomon is shopping for real talent.

The answer is Jerusalem. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, says the craftsman from Tyre will work with his craftsmen "…in Judah and Jerusalem…" He adds that his father David provided them. So the visiting expert joins a team that's already in place, and nobody has to work alone.

The answer is False. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, tells Hiram, king of Tyre, "…my servants will work with yours…" The two crews are meant to work side by side. Solomon is asking for teamwork, not a hand-off.

The answer is wheat, barley, wine and oil. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, promises Hiram's woodcutters 20,000 cors of ground wheat, 20,000 cors of barley, 20,000 baths of wine and 20,000 baths of olive oil. So the pay comes in grain, wine and oil, and there's plenty of it. Solomon plans to pay for what he asks.

The answer is because the LORD loves His people. Hiram, king of Tyre, writes back to Solomon, David's son and Israel's king: "Because the LORD loves His people, He has set you over them as king." Hiram points to the LORD's love for His people and nothing else. Not bad for the first lines of a business letter.

The answer is True. Hiram, king of Tyre, writes, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who made the heavens and the earth! He has given King David a wise son with insight and understanding…" That wise son is Solomon, who is getting the letter. Hiram put it in writing, friends. That's a nice thing to find in the mail.

The answer is Dan. Hiram, king of Tyre, says Huram-abi, the craftsman he's sending, is "…the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan…" His father is a man of Tyre. So his mother comes from the daughters of Dan, and his father is from Tyre.

The answer is False. Hiram, king of Tyre, describes Huram-abi as skilled in gold, silver, bronze and iron. But the list keeps going: stone, wood, colored yarn and fine linen. He can also execute any design he's given. That resume would not fit on one page.

The answer is float them as rafts by sea. Hiram, king of Tyre, says, "We will cut logs from Lebanon, as many as you need, and we will float them to you as rafts by sea down to Joppa." So the logs ride the water instead of a road. I think that beats carrying them one at a time. Solomon can take them up to Jerusalem from there.

The answer is Joppa. Hiram, king of Tyre, says his men will float the logs as rafts by sea "…down to Joppa." From there, Solomon can take them up to Jerusalem. So Joppa is where the sea trip ends and the next leg begins.
